summary:
Schleswig-Holstein stands under the German national framework. Legal gender recognition runs through the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), in force since 1 November 2024, under which a prisoner's placement tracks the legal gender entry unless state law provides an exclusion.

No Schleswig-Holstein statute or ordinance specific to trans people is in force. The state has no prison act provision of its own governing the placement of trans prisoners, so the SBGG mechanics and the national July 2026 placement case are the operative rules for a visitor detained here.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure. In July 2026 a German court sent a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement, whose legal gender had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act, to a men's prison, amid public outcry over women's-prison safety. The case drove the Länder-level prison-placement law debate and illustrates how placement can diverge from the legal gender entry in practice.

A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 raises constitutional doubts about trans-targeted exception clauses in Länder prison law, though Schleswig-Holstein has not enacted such a clause.
tangentialFactors:
Schleswig-Holstein was one of five states, alongside Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Saarland, to table a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019. Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia supported the motion and Bavaria indicated potential support with modifications; the Bundestag approved the federal ban on 7 May 2020 with backing from every party except the AfD.

Nationally, a ban on conversion therapy for minors has been in force since May 2020, carrying penalties of up to one year in prison and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.
localsOnly:
Residents detained in Schleswig-Holstein prisons are housed under the national SBGG placement rule, with no state-specific statute modifying it. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006.

The German STOP the HATE campaign maintains a counselling finder, an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation and reporting channels.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Schleswig-Holstein prison administrations apply the SBGG placement rule in practice, and how intake review is conducted, is not sourced in the inventory and remains unresolved.

The Verfassungsblog analysis raises constitutional doubts about trans-targeted exception clauses in Länder law, but whether such challenges have been litigated to a decision is not sourced here.
